true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Downsize loop can corrupt or ignore failures, and mishandles animated GIFs

The return value of `downsize` is ignored, so if convert fails the loop repeats 5 times for nothing. The in-place conversion (from == to) on a tempfile can also lose the original. After downsizing, `tempfile.size` may be stale, because `File#size` on a Tempfile can be cached or buffered. The upload then uses the old size. For GIFs the gifsicle path uses `--resize-fit` with "80%", which is not a valid dimension argument, so it fails. If the image is still too big after the loop, the upload goes ahead and is later rejected with a confusing error.

The full URL path is also not a valid targetOrigin, which must be an origin, so postMessage silently fails to deliver for any referer containing a path. true_positives.golden_comment: The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Embed access control relies on the spoofable Referer header and ALLOWALL framing

It is also often stripped by privacy settings or Referrer-Policy, so legitimate embeds fail. The response then sets X-Frame-Options to ALLOWALL, which removes clickjacking protection for the page. A logged-in user visiting a malicious page could be framed. Because current_user is used, the framed content can include user-specific data.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
align-items mixin emits invalid legacy-prefixed values

The mixin passes the same `$alignment` to every vendor property. The old `-webkit-box-align` accepts `start`, `end`, `center`, `baseline` and `stretch`. `-ms-flex-align` accepts `start`, `end`, `center`, `baseline` and `stretch`. Neither accepts `flex-start` or `flex-end`, so those values would produce invalid declarations on older browsers. The bare `-ms-align-items` is not a real property. For the `center` and `baseline` values used in this PR the output is fine, but the mixin is unsafe for other values.

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

false_positives.candidate:
Public members endpoint response shape changed, breaking existing consumers

`GET /groups/:id/members` used to return a bare array of users. It now returns `{members: [...], meta: {...}}` and defaults to 50 results. Any other client of this endpoint (plugins, other JS callers, API users) will break. The old automatic-group-only limit workaround is also gone, so non-automatic groups are now silently capped at 50 for callers that don't paginate. No controller spec covers the new response shape or pagination.

Unvalidated limit and offset parameters

`limit` comes straight from `params[:limit].to_i` with no upper bound, so a client can request an arbitrarily large page and load the whole group. A negative limit or offset can also cause a database error (negative OFFSET raises in Postgres), resulting in a 500.

addMembers never clears the input and ignores errors

After `addMembers`, the usernames field is not cleared (there is a TODO), so clicking Add twice re-sends the same names. The returned promise has no failure handler, so server errors such as the 422 for automatic groups are silent.

remove_member deletes via the association with a raw id and skips group-level cleanup

`group.users.delete(user_id)` is passed an integer. This works for has_many :through, but it bypasses `Group#remove`, and any callbacks or counters tied to it. Elsewhere in the code `group.add` is used for adds, so removal is inconsistent. A non-member id is also silently ignored. The spec for this path only checks the simple case.

true_positives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
ensure_loaded! reads @loaded_locales before the mutex, and the cache key ignores fallbacks

`ensure_loaded!` reads and initializes `@loaded_locales` outside LOAD_MUTEX, and `load_locale` does the same. Another thread's `reload!` can reset the array to `[]` mid-call, and a concurrent request can race on it. Separately, `translate` caches by `key+locale+backend`. With fallbacks, a cached result may have come from the fallback locale, or the cache may be stale after the site default locale changes. The cache is never invalidated when `SiteSetting.default_locale` changes.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).
In UsernameForm.authenticate(), isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is called without passing the required UserModel parameter.

With isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) requiring user != null, authenticate(...) will not call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) on the initial login page where context.getUser() is still null, so conditional passkey UI will not be set up for first-time passkey login. Consider whether this should also be enabled when no user has been selected yet so ID-less passkey authentication on the initial login form continues to work.

false_positives.candidate:
Catch of a generic Exception swallows the test's own failure

The try block calls fail(...) when the webauth form is found. fail() throws AssertionError, which is an Error, so it is not caught by catch(Exception). The nullValue() assertion on a findElement result would also throw NoSuchElementException, so the check is convoluted. If an element is present, the nullValue assertion throws AssertionError, which propagates correctly. The real concern is the catch of all Exceptions, which hides unrelated driver errors. Use findElements().isEmpty() instead.

Missing @Override on overriding method

shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators overrides the parent method but has no @Override annotation. If the parent signature changes, the override silently stops working.

Passkey form attributes are set on a form that is not used for the username-only login page

The branch around line 115 now calls webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) when a user is already set. fillContextForm sets a new challenge auth note and sets attributes on context.form(). UsernameForm now skips its success shortcut and falls through to super.authenticate in that case. That is the intended re-authentication path. However, this means the challenge note is overwritten on every re-render, including after a failed password attempt. A passkey page left open in another tab then fails challenge validation. This is a minor robustness issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative offset slicing on Django queryset raises an error or is unsafe

OptimizedCursorPaginator passes a user-controlled negative cursor.offset straight into queryset[start_offset:stop]. Django querysets do not support negative indexing and raise AssertionError (a 500). The comment claiming the ORM handles it is wrong. The cursor offset comes from the request cursor string, which Cursor.from_string parses with no sign check. The 'authorization' for this path is only a client-supplied query flag plus a role check, so the feature is an unvalidated attack surface that was never needed.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Authorization check may fail or be too broad

organization_context.member can be None (for example for superusers who are not members), which raises AttributeError. The `or` short-circuits for superusers, but a non-member with other access would crash. Gating a pagination mode on is_superuser or global access is also weak protection for the unsafe negative-offset path. Trailing whitespace on lines 71 and 89 also exists.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New paginator is mostly duplicated code and has no tests

OptimizedCursorPaginator copies BasePaginator.get_result nearly verbatim, and get_item_key and value_from_cursor duplicate Paginator. It adds no real optimization. No tests cover the new paginator, the negative offset path, or the endpoint flag. Also get_item_key uses math.floor on a datetime, since order_by is -datetime, which raises TypeError. The optimized path therefore breaks on the audit log endpoint it is wired to.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Importing non-existent OptimizedCursorPaginator

false_positives.candidate:
Shared BasePaginator now lets negative offsets through for prev cursors

The change in BasePaginator.get_result uses the raw offset when cursor.is_prev. A crafted prev cursor with a negative offset on any paginator that uses BasePaginator (many endpoints) now reaches queryset slicing with a negative start and raises an AssertionError. Previously the slice used offset directly, and a negative offset failed the same way, but the comment claims this is a deliberate feature. The edit is not behavior-preserving in intent and adds no validation. The same pattern is duplicated in the new class, and `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` uses the unclamped offset.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative offsets passed to Django queryset slicing

OptimizedCursorPaginator slices the queryset with a negative start (`queryset[start_offset:stop]` where start_offset = cursor.offset < 0). Django raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` on negative slices, so a crafted cursor such as `?cursor=0:-5:0` causes a 500. The comment claiming the ORM handles this is wrong. The cursor is user-controlled via Cursor.from_string, which accepts negative offsets.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BasePaginator now permits negative offsets for prev cursors

The change `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` lets a prev cursor with a negative offset reach `queryset[negative:stop]`. Before this change it was the same failure mode, but the new code is explicitly intended to allow it, so it affects every paginator subclass. The result is an AssertionError/500 for any endpoint that accepts a crafted `is_prev` cursor. The later `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` check also uses the unclamped offset.

false_negatives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

false_positives.candidate:
Eviction is based on a stale span_count and the redirect limit was reduced

span_count is only set when a zunionstore ran, so a zadd done earlier in Python can leave the count out of date. It is only recomputed with zcard when it is 0. After a merge, span_count is the size of the last union, which is correct, but the first merge's count is overwritten. The redirect loop limit was also silently cut from 10000 to 1000, which means deeper trees are no longer joined correctly. Evicting with zpopmin drops the oldest spans silently, with no metric.

Hard dependency on end_timestamp_precise

`val["end_timestamp_precise"]` raises KeyError for any span payload missing the field, which crashes the whole batch in the consumer. Using `.get` with a fallback would be safer.

Removed max_segment_spans enforcement while the parameter remains

The span-count check in _load_segment_data was removed, but `max_segment_spans` is still a constructor parameter and is now unused. The Lua script hardcodes 1000 instead of using the configured value. Configuration therefore has no effect.

Undocumented opt-in flag that unlocks a less-validated paginator

Any org member with global access, or any superuser, can pass `optimized_pagination=true` to switch to a paginator that is meant to allow negative offsets. This is an unnecessary expansion of the attack surface on the audit-log endpoint. The paginator is also not tested, and a comment about 'permissions checked at the queryset level' does not justify skipping offset validation. The trailing whitespace on lines 71 and 89 is a minor nit.

true_positives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test factory silently swallows all exceptions and rewrites sample_rate for all store_event callers

The bare `except Exception: pass` blocks hide errors. The helper also changes sample_rate for any test event that carries the error_sampling context, a global change to fixtures. Also, a client_sample_rate of 0 is ignored because the check is truthiness.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache key uses Python hash() of project IDs, which is not stable or collision-free

hash(tuple(...)) of ints is deterministic within a process, but a 64-bit hash makes collisions possible. Two different project sets could then share an eligibility result, so a non-allowlisted project could be upsampled, or the reverse. The key is built from the hash instead of the joined IDs, so it is not safe as a cross-process cache key. Build the key from the joined sorted IDs instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling check uses the outer dataset and request query rather than the scoped dataset and actual query

The check passes the closure's `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`, and it inspects request.GET['query'] instead of the `query` parameter. The dashboard-widget split paths call _get_event_stats with discover and a rewritten query such as '!event.type:transaction'. In those paths the decision is wrong, so transaction queries could get upsampled_count (sample_weight does not exist for transactions), or error queries could be missed. The check is also repeated on every call. Also, 'event.type:error' is matched as a substring of the query text, which misses queries like '!event.type:error' and similar forms.

false_positives.candidate:
Cache invalidation is never called, so the cache is stale for up to 60s

invalidate_upsampling_cache is defined but nothing calls it, and it only deletes a single project-set key. Changes to the allowlist option therefore do not take effect until the 60s TTL expires. The docstring claiming consistency is misleading. The caching also saves almost nothing, because options.get is already cheap.

Stray submodule/gitlink file added to the PR

The 'sentry-repo' file is a subproject commit pointer unrelated to the feature. It should not be committed.

Tests mock the whole options module and depend on factory behavior, with no cache coverage

Mocking `options` makes every options.get return the allowlist, which affects unrelated lookups. The cache is never cleared between tests, and the key is identical for identical project sets, so tests can leak state. The caching, the invalidate function, and the top_events path are untested.

Transform only handles an exact 'count()' and always aliases the result as 'count'

Other count forms and aggregates are not handled, such as count() with an alias, or equations. Rewriting to 'upsampled_count() as count' can also collide with a user-requested column that is already named count. Events lacking sample_weight (older events, or events without a client sample rate) would sum to 0, so the chart would undercount. The comments claim the schema guarantees the column, but nothing enforces that.

Upsampling is applied to RPC datasets, but the transform produces a legacy-only function

In the RPC paths (spans_rpc and ourlogs), the transform emits 'upsampled_count() as count'. This is only defined in the discover SnQL function converter. The helper returns False for those datasets, so the path is dead code today, but it would break if the helper changes.

upsampled_count is registered as a public function for all discover queries

It is not marked private. Users can call it directly against transactions or non-allowlisted projects, where sample_weight is missing, and get errors or wrong results. It also sums sample_weight without the sampling-rate inversion (1/rate), so the semantics are unclear.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error events are paired with the wrong ids and the zero-ts default breaks ordering

`zip(error_ids, events.values())` assumes get_multi returns results in the same order as error_ids, which a dict does not guarantee. Events can therefore be mislabeled, and the id field is unreliable. Missing timestamps default to 0.0, which sorts those errors first. The endpoint also now runs a Snuba query before pagination, and request.user.id is passed even for anonymous users.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.

Table widget renders empty data under the feature flag

When `use-table-widget-visualization` is enabled, TableWidgetVisualization receives hardcoded `columns=[]` and empty `tableData`. Every table widget shows empty, ignoring result.data and result.meta. The `loading` state is also dropped.

true_positives.golden_comment: Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Truthiness check on initial_data misses age=0 or timestamp=0

validate_timestamp and validate_age use `if self.initial_data.get(...)`, which is falsy for 0. A report with age=0 plus a timestamp passes validation even though the specs are meant to be mutually exclusive. Use `in` or `is not None` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Analytics recorded before the feature flag check

analytics.record runs before the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` feature check. Events are therefore emitted for orgs that do not have the feature, and the request is then rejected with 404.

false_positives.candidate:
Default autofix automation tuning changed from low to off

This changes the default behaviour for every project without an explicit option value. Autofix automation silently turns off for existing projects that relied on the default. The change is bundled into an unrelated PR with no migration or release note.

Editing already-merged migrations to no-ops

Migrations 0917 and 0920 are rewritten to do nothing, and their tests are deleted. Any environment that already ran the original bodies keeps the data they produced. The comment says the migration was never run, but that cannot be guaranteed. The comment also refers to a 0921 migration that is not part of this diff.

New comment template drops culprit and changes markdown list formatting

true_positives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Component is misnamed TwoFactor

The default export in BackupCode.tsx is named `TwoFactor`, which duplicates the name of the other component and is confusing in stack traces and devtools.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code check has no format validation and a non-atomic consume

`credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` is compared with plain `indexOf`. This is not constant-time, though that is minor. More importantly, consuming the code is a read-modify-write, so two concurrent requests with the same code can both succeed. Also, the existing condition `user.password && !credentials.totpCode` skips the password check whenever totpCode is empty. Passing a backupCode with no totpCode therefore works, but a TOTP code with a wrong password still skips the password check. This pre-existing behavior is now extended by the backup path.

true_positives.golden_comment: Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Modal state and the blob URL are not cleaned up after the backup codes are shown

resetState does not clear backupCodes, the blob URL, the secret or dataUri. The object URL is never revoked on close or unmount, so a leak remains. The plaintext codes also stay in component state after the dialog closes. Also, onOpenChange (clicking the overlay or pressing Esc) closes the dialog on the backup codes step without calling resetState, so the next open may resume at the backup codes step.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup codes are overwritten and returned before 2FA is enabled

The setup endpoint generates new backup codes, persists them and returns them in plaintext, all before the TOTP code is verified. If a user cancels setup, the stored codes remain on the account. Because twoFactorEnabled is false, they are unused for now, but they stay valid secrets. If 2FA is later enabled by another path, they apply. Codes should be generated at enable time, or cleared when setup is cancelled.

Disable endpoint does not guard against non-string backupCode or malformed data

`req.body.backupCode.replaceAll(...)` throws a 500 if backupCode is not a string, for example a number or an object sent in the JSON body. `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` is also unguarded. Validate that the input is a string first. In addition, consumed codes are nulled in the login flow, and `indexOf` on user input could match a null or empty entry if the input is odd.

Lost access toggle button lacks type="button"

The Button defaults to type submit inside the Form, so clicking 'Lost access' or 'Go back' may submit the form. The submit would carry validation of the required fields, such as the backup code, and could trigger an unwanted disable request. Set type="button". The same applies to the Cancel button.

Event type destination calendar overrides the organizer's, and the first item is persisted as the booking's

Inconsistent e2e expectations for destinationCalendar

Team destination calendars lost when the organizer has none

Computed zod keys are bogus, so the minimal schema is wrong

`[z.string().toString()]` evaluates to the string "[object Object]" or similar. The schema therefore requires a numeric property with that literal name, so `safeParse` fails on real token responses whenever credential sync is on. Zod objects strip unknown keys by default, so data such as `expiry_date` or `refresh_token` is dropped. The intended 'any number is the expiry' logic does not exist; it needs `.passthrough()` or `catchall`.

parseRefreshTokenResponse result stored as the key

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test relies on real sleep after patching time.sleep

monkeypatch replaces time.sleep globally with a no-op, so the added `time.sleep(0.1)` does nothing. The test remains racy because the flusher thread may not have flushed before join. The new limit test only checks the process-to-shard mapping, not restarts or any flush behavior.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() deadline logic skips terminating remaining processes

When the deadline expires, the loop breaks and the remaining processes are never terminated. Also, `deadline = time.time() + timeout if timeout else None` treats timeout=0 as no deadline, so join waits forever.

false_positives.candidate:
Restarted flusher gets a new SpansBuffer, losing state of the old one

Every restart in _create_process_for_shards builds a new SpansBuffer(shards) and overwrites self.buffers[process_index]. Any in-memory state on the old buffer is dropped. Previously the same buffer was reused across restarts. Also, the old thread (in produce_to_pipe/test mode) is never stopped on restart, so two threads can flush the same shards.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its docstring

The docstring says errors don't block offset commits, but the assertion is `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`. The test passes when nothing is committed, which hides the intended behaviour. It also only waits 2s for a 1s commit loop, so it can pass vacuously.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

false_positives.candidate:
Commit happens from a background thread, and state is shared across partition assignments

The Arroyo `commit` callable is invoked from a separate thread, but Arroyo strategies are expected to call commit from the main consumer thread. The FixedQueuePool and OffsetTracker are created once by the factory and shared across every `create_with_partitions` call. After a rebalance, stale offsets and `last_committed` from revoked partitions persist. Items still queued from the old strategy can later be committed for partitions no longer owned. Also, `close()` on the strategy shuts down the shared pool, so the next strategy created by the factory after a rebalance gets a dead pool with no workers.

Python's hash() on str is randomized per process, so group assignment is not stable

`hash(group_key)` uses per-process hash randomization (PYTHONHASHSEED). Within one process the mapping is consistent, so in-process ordering holds. But the 'consistent hashing' docstring is misleading, and the assignment changes on every restart or rebalance. Use a stable hash such as crc32 or md5 if per-queue behaviour must be reproducible.

Unbounded queues give no backpressure; docstring claims otherwise

The queues are unbounded and `submit` never blocks or raises `MessageRejected`. The consumer will keep polling Kafka while a slow worker backs up, so memory grows without limit. The class docstring's claim of 'natural backpressure' is false.

Worker uses queue.ShutDown, which exists only in Python 3.13+

`queue.ShutDown` and `Queue.shutdown()` were added in Python 3.13. On earlier versions, `except queue.ShutDown` raises AttributeError and `q.shutdown` fails. The shutdown path swallows the failure via `except Exception`, so workers blocked in `get()` never wake. Shutdown then waits out the join timeout and leaves daemon threads behind. Also, `break` inside the `except queue.ShutDown` around `result_processor` skips nothing useful but is misplaced.

get_committable_offsets scans a Python range over offsets

The loop iterates `range(start, max_offset+1)` under a lock every second. If offsets have large gaps (compacted or filtered topics), this becomes a very long loop. A gap also stops commits permanently, since a missing offset is never in all_offsets. For example, a skipped or non-contiguous offset blocks all further commits for that partition.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denied checks on cached permissions requery the DB each time

When the cached permissions do not allow the request, the code always calls getIdentityPermissions, which hits the DB. The denial cache is only populated after that call succeeds, so a burst of concurrent denied checks for different resources causes a DB query per distinct resource. Distinct names also each get their own denial key, so the cache gives little protection against scanning patterns. Metrics also count a cache miss in this case.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key collides with the permission cache key

userPermDenialCacheKey is namespace+".perm_"+userUID+"_"+action+"_"+name+"_"+parent. userPermCacheKey is namespace+".perm_"+userUID+"_"+action. The prefixes are the same, and both are stored in the same underlying cache. Underscore-joined fields with no separator escaping are also ambiguous: names containing underscores could collide with other users' or actions' keys. Use a distinct prefix such as ".perm_denied_" and an unambiguous separator.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache blocks newly granted access for the TTL, defeating the PR goal

A denial is cached for 30s per (user, action, name, folder). If a check runs just before a resource is created or permissions are granted, for example a creator checking a dashboard before the permission row is visible, access stays denied for the full TTL even though the permission now exists in the DB. The fallback requery is skipped on every denial-cache hit. Nothing invalidates the entry when permissions change.

Errors from the cached-permission lookup are ignored

getCachedIdentityPermissions can return a real error, such as a failure in GetUserIdentifiers. Check treats every error as a cache miss and falls through, which is acceptable. However, the err variable is shadowed inside the if block, and List does the same. The resulting double lookup of identifiers is a minor inefficiency.

Missing test that a denial is cached after a DB-checked deny

The tests never verify that Check populates permDenialCache after a denial, or that a repeat call avoids the DB. The 'should return permissions from cache' case in getUserPermissions was removed without equivalent coverage of the singleflight and DB paths.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing React key on GrafanaRuleListItem in list map

The old GrafanaRuleLoader usage passed `key={key}`, but the new `<GrafanaRuleListItem>` in the `rules.map` has no key. React will warn about missing keys. Reconciliation by index can also mix up item state (delete modal, silence drawer, redirect state) as the list grows or changes. Add `key={key}`.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence drawer unreachable for prom-only Grafana rules

The silence drawer renders only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)`. In the list view `rule` is now undefined, since only `promRule` is passed. The AlertRuleMenu now shows 'Silence notifications' via prom abilities, but clicking it sets `showSilenceDrawer` and nothing renders. Silencing is silently broken from the list view.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete menu item hidden when only promRule is available

The Delete item renders only when `canDelete && rulerRule`. In the list view there is no rulerRule, so Delete never appears even for users with permission. Duplicate and export work, so this is an inconsistent regression. The `handleDelete` signature also requires a RulerRuleDTO.

Stale comment and variable name after ruler prefetch removal

The comment above this block still says it preloads ruler rules, and the variable is still named `cacheAndRulerPreload`, but the ruler prefetch was removed. Update both to reflect cache-only behavior.

returnTo dropped from rule view link

The previous list item built the href with `createReturnTo()` as a `returnTo` param. The new href omits it, so the back navigation from the rule view page no longer returns to the list view.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Assertion on call count 5 is brittle and encodes the double interpolation

toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5) hard-codes the number of redundant applyTemplateVariables calls (1 outer, then 4 inner, one per sub-request). It makes the double interpolation look intentional, and it will break when the group sizing changes.

Queries are interpolated twice in the shard path

runShardSplitQuery now interpolates each target with applyTemplateVariables. It then passes the already-interpolated targets, via runSplitQuery at line 163, into code that applies applyTemplateVariables to each target again. Double interpolation can corrupt values that contain `$` or escaped characters after the first pass, and it duplicates ad-hoc filter injection. Adhoc filters may be added twice to the expression. It also costs extra work for every shard sub-request. The test change that expects applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times shows the repeated calls. Interpolate once at the top level and skip it in the inner runSplitQuery, for example with an option.

applyTemplateVariables may mutate the original request targets

The map result replaces the targets, but the tests' mocks of applyTemplateVariables mutate and return the input query. If the real implementation returns shared objects, request.targets gets modified. Later retries and sub-requests would then see interpolated expressions. trackGroupedQueries receives the original request, which could end up inconsistent. Callers may also depend on the un-interpolated targets.

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Plugin request log loses traceID

The old logRequest explicitly added a traceID (via tracing.TraceIDFromContext) to the log params, and that code was removed. The new code relies on m.logger.FromContext(ctx). That only adds traceID if the infra logger's context hooks inject it, and the diff does not show that they do. If they don't, the 'Plugin Request Completed' logs silently lose their trace correlation. The PR does not mention or test this change.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.

false_positives.candidate:
FromContext fallback drops context attributes

If the type assertion fails, the code returns d.New(), which silently discards the context-derived attributes. The failure is not logged, so the logger has no endpoint or plugin fields and the loss is invisible.

Stale function name and no tests for the new middleware

The helper is still called instrumentContext even though it now lives in the contextual logger middleware, which the rename was meant to clean up. The new ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no tests, and the moved behavior (logger attributes added to the context, and logging order relative to the other middlewares) is not covered anywhere.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert (TOCTOU)

CreateOrUpdateDevice counts devices and then inserts in separate statements with no transaction or lock. Concurrent requests from new devices can all see count < limit and all insert, so the limit can be exceeded. It also issues a COUNT query on every uncached tag when a limit is set.

true_positives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Tagging moved from an async goroutine to the synchronous auth path

TagDevice, which does DB reads and writes, now runs inline in Authenticate. Every anonymous request that misses the cache pays that latency. A slow or failing database now delays or blocks anonymous page loads, which previously completed independently of tagging. The request context is also now used, so a client cancellation aborts the tagging.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached for any zero-row update

A zero-row update does not necessarily mean the limit was reached for a new device. It can also happen for a device last updated more than 30 days ago or just outside the time window. A returning-but-expired device is rejected, and Authenticate then fails with a generic error rather than a clear limit message.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache entry set before the DB write, so a rejected device is cached as tagged

tagDeviceUI calls localCache.SetDefault(key) before CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached (or any DB error), the key stays cached for 29 minutes. The next request from that device then returns nil and is silently allowed through. The limit is therefore enforced only on the first request per device per cache window, and transient DB errors also cause skipped tagging.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Limit test covers only the rejection of a new device

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit checks only that a second new device is rejected. It does not check that an existing device can still update at the limit, that the limit=0 path is unlimited, or the client.go behaviour of returning the error. impl_test and the client tests were not extended.

Tagging moved from an async goroutine to the synchronous auth path

TagDevice, which does DB reads and writes, now runs inline in Authenticate. Every anonymous request that misses the cache pays that latency. A slow or failing database now delays or blocks anonymous page loads, which previously completed independently of tagging. The request context is also now used, so a client cancellation aborts the tagging.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Debug logging at Error level that dumps all IDs on every batch

Each batch logs at Error level, including the full `ids` slice (up to the batch size, which may be tens of thousands of IDs) and the condition. This also happens when nothing was found. The same pattern appears at lines 537, 554, 557, 576 and 579. It floods error logs and triggers alerting on error logs during normal operation. Use Debug level and drop the ID list. Also, the 'err' value logged is always nil at that point.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute

The ticker was reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This looks like a leftover debugging change unrelated to the deadlock fix. All cleanup jobs (snapshots, dashboard versions, annotations, query history and others) will run 10x more often. Each run can last up to the 9 minute timeout, so runs may nearly back to back and add DB load. Revert it to 10 minutes.

false_positives.candidate:
Orphan tag cleanup condition is ambiguous inside fetchIDs

The condition `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM annotation a WHERE annotation_id = a.id)` is now used in `SELECT id FROM annotation_tag WHERE ...`. The unqualified `annotation_id` resolves to annotation_tag only because annotation has no such column, which is fragile. More importantly, the `id` column of annotation_tag is used for the delete. That is correct only if the table has an id column, so verify that it does.

SQLite parameter-limit check uses configured batch size and misses the placeholder cap

The inline-ID branch triggers only when the configured batch size is above 999. The decision should be based on len(ids). With a small configured value the placeholders path is fine, but the check depends on config rather than on the actual number of parameters. Also, for MaxCount cleanup, LimitOffset may return up to the batch size, so the logic is consistent only by coincidence. Prefer checking len(ids).

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete stores the wrong logger in the context

klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) is used instead of the enriched `log`. The method, name and kind values are lost for downstream logging, and the async legacy goroutine inherits this context.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Async legacy DeleteCollection recorded as storage duration

The goroutine that calls Legacy.DeleteCollection records its outcome with recordStorageDuration. It should use recordLegacyDuration, so the legacy metric is never emitted for delete-collection and the storage metric is polluted.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete success metric uses name as the kind label

On successful delete, recordStorageDuration is passed `name` where every other call passes options.Kind. This creates a high-cardinality label series per object name and splits the metrics for this method.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy write reuses the request context

The goroutines derive their context from the request ctx. Once the HTTP request completes, that ctx is cancelled, so the legacy create/update/delete may be cancelled mid-flight or fail immediately. The legacy write is not reliable. Use context.WithoutCancel(ctx), or a background context that carries the logger, for the legacy write. Update's goroutine also reuses objInfo and the validation closures after the request has returned, and legacy failures are only recorded in metrics, not logged.

Storage failures recorded as legacy duration metrics

When Storage.Create fails (line 45) and when Storage.Update fails (line 129), the code calls recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration. Unified-storage errors are therefore attributed to the legacy metrics, and the storage error metrics miss them.

Tests don't verify async legacy writes

The tests never wait for or assert that the legacy mock is called after the unified write. The legacy mocks are set up but unverified, and the goroutines may outlive the test or race with mock state. The error case sets up a Legacy Create expectation that is never used.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No re-check of cache after taking write lock (thundering herd)

After the RLock check misses, every concurrent caller takes the write lock and then reloads the manifest from disk. The cache is not re-checked under the write lock. On a cold start, N concurrent requests will each read and parse assets-manifest.json serially. Re-check `entryPointAssetsCache != nil && cfg.Env != setting.Dev` after `Lock()` to avoid the duplicate work.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache overwritten with nil result on error

`entryPointAssetsCache = result` runs even when `err != nil`, in which case result is nil. A transient read failure therefore wipes a previously valid cache, which matters in Dev mode, where the code reloads on every call. Callers also receive a nil assets pointer alongside the error. The cache should only be assigned when err == nil.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false, with confusing dead logic

The function computes `enabled := !IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns false on both branches. It is unconditionally disabled regardless of the feature flag. That is the intended security fix, but the inverted flag check and the redundant branches look like a bug and mislead readers into thinking the flag still controls the feature. It should be a plain `return false` with a comment explaining why. The error message 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' also gives users no hint that the feature was deliberately disabled.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

false_positives.candidate:
No tests cover the disabled behaviour

The PR changes SQL expression behaviour to always fail but adds no test asserting that QueryTypeSQL returns an error and that the stub DB errors. Any existing SQL expression tests that expect success will now fail or silently go stale.

SQL expressions are still reachable through the non-reader path

Only ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery is gated. UnmarshalSQLCommand in sql_command.go (used by the legacy node-building path) still calls NewSQLCommand, and nothing in that path checks the flag or the disabled state. Because the stub DB returns 'not implemented' from TablesList, those queries fail rather than execute. Still, the disabling is incidental to the stub and not enforced at the entry point. Add an explicit guard in NewSQLCommand or UnmarshalSQLCommand.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Concurrent builds of same key can race and leak/overwrite index

Removing the lock around the whole of BuildIndex means two concurrent builds for the same key can both run. For file-backed indexes, `bleve.New(dir)` fails for the second caller because the directory already exists. For memory indexes, the second build silently overwrites the first in the cache and leaks it. `getOrCreateIndex` is a check-then-build with no dedup. Previously the lock serialized this.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates cache without lock

`TotalDocs` reads `b.cache` without taking `cacheMu`. Builds can now write to the map concurrently, and `init` calls `TotalDocs` in a new log line. A concurrent map read and write can cause a fatal runtime error.

false_positives.candidate:
Blocking Init in constructor with a cancelable background ctx; stale/hanging failure modes

NewResourceServer now runs the full search index build synchronously, so construction blocks until every namespace is indexed. If anything fails, the whole server fails to construct. Previously this failure only surfaced on the first request. The lifecycle `Init` also runs here with the server's own context. Startup time and failure semantics change significantly, and the PR's own question about lazy-init dependents remains unanswered. The `Init` call to `lifecycle.Init` can also run before the SQL backend has been set up by other callers.

Data race on shared err and counter in init workers

The errgroup closures run concurrently. They all assign to the outer `err` with `_, _, err = s.build(...)`, and they all do `totalBatchesIndexed++` without synchronization. This is a data race, and it is now on the startup path. The reported `namespaced_indexed` count can also be wrong. Use a local error variable and an atomic counter.

Test skipped for postgres instead of fixed

The integration test is now skipped for postgres to work around a failure that is probably caused by the eager init change. This reduces coverage rather than addressing the cause.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup registered with the literal alias "alias"

getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove) uses the literal string "alias" instead of the created alias, so the IDPs are never cleaned up. This can leak state into other tests. The same bug appears for idp-alias-20.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Org-filter searchKey does not capture the cached result's dependence on the organizationId

The cache key is only realm+mode, and the searchKey is the organizationId. IdentityProviderListQuery stores one entry per searchKey. When an org changes membership of an IDP, only the three login keys are invalidated, which is fine. However, the query is built per search key and an IDP's enabled/org state may change via organization enable/disable or removal of an org, with no login invalidation. Org-bound IDPs are wrapped for isEnabled, but removing an org or unlinking an IDP through the organization provider can leave stale lists. getById invalidation of the IDP id does not invalidate the list query.

Update invalidation relies on a possibly stale or null original model

update() calls getById(model.getInternalId()), which may return the cached model. The login predicate is evaluated on that. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate calls getLoginPredicate on `original` and `updated`. The predicate reads idp.getConfig().get(...), which could NPE if the config is null. Also, if the model is returned wrapped, the enabled state reflects the organization's state, so the original's enabled state is misjudged (an org-disabled IDP looks disabled), which can skip a needed invalidation.

getLoginPredicate semantics changed without matching the search options

The predicate now also requires org-linked IDPs to have BROKER_PUBLIC=true. getLoginSearchOptions is unchanged, and other callers of getLoginPredicate get new filtering behavior. Also, idp.getConfig() may be null, causing an NPE.

remove() now fetches the IDP unconditionally and may NPE

storedIdp = idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias) can be null for a nonexistent alias. registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp) is safe because the predicate checks nonNull, but the isInvalid branch still calls registerIDPInvalidation(storedIdp), which throws an NPE on null (previous behavior was the same). The added DB query on every remove is also needless when the cache branch is taken.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default KeyStore's provider

The method returns the provider of the default KeyStore type, which is SUN, not BouncyCastle. Callers that use `BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER` can end up with a mismatched provider name. This is misleading and is likely to break when other CryptoProvider methods are invoked in the authz-client.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code: redundant ASN1 encodings

The two `ASN1Encoder.create().write(...)` calls at lines 114-115 discard their results and do nothing. They are leftovers and should be removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
readSequence loop mishandles indefinite length and can loop forever

readLength() returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding, so the `while (length > 0)` loop is skipped and an empty list is returned without any error. Separately, if readNext() returns a zero-length array, `length` never decreases and the loop does not terminate. Truncated or malformed signatures are therefore not rejected cleanly.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

`order()` is added as an abstract interface method without a default. Any third-party or other-module CryptoProvider implementation will fail to compile. Providing `default int order() { return 0; }` would avoid the break.

false_positives.candidate:
Incorrect length bound check

The out-of-bounds check is only done for long-form lengths, and the comparison `length >= limit` is against the whole input rather than the remaining bytes. Short-form lengths are never checked. The subsequent `new byte[length]` in read() can therefore be sized by malformed input, with failure only at EOF. Inside nested decoders, `limit` is the size of the sub-array, which makes the check inconsistent.

Ties between providers resolved silently and nondeterministically

The check that rejected multiple providers was removed. Providers with equal order (e.g. Default, Elytron and FIPS are all 200) are now chosen by ServiceLoader order, so a misconfigured classpath no longer fails fast. The ignored providers are logged only at debug level.

Python's hash() on str is randomized per process, so group assignment is not stable

`hash(group_key)` uses per-process hash randomization (PYTHONHASHSEED). Within one process the mapping is consistent, so in-process ordering holds. But the 'consistent hashing' docstring is misleading, and the assignment changes on every restart or rebalance. Use a stable hash such as crc32 or md5 if per-queue behaviour must be reproducible.

Worker uses queue.ShutDown, which exists only in Python 3.13+

`queue.ShutDown` and `Queue.shutdown()` were added in Python 3.13. On earlier versions, `except queue.ShutDown` raises AttributeError and `q.shutdown` fails. The shutdown path swallows the failure via `except Exception`, so workers blocked in `get()` never wake. Shutdown then waits out the join timeout and leaves daemon threads behind. Also, `break` inside the `except queue.ShutDown` around `result_processor` skips nothing useful but is misplaced.

Commit happens from a background thread, and state is shared across partition assignments

The Arroyo `commit` callable is invoked from a separate thread, but Arroyo strategies are expected to call commit from the main consumer thread. The FixedQueuePool and OffsetTracker are created once by the factory and shared across every `create_with_partitions` call. After a rebalance, stale offsets and `last_committed` from revoked partitions persist. Items still queued from the old strategy can later be committed for partitions no longer owned. Also, `close()` on the strategy shuts down the shared pool, so the next strategy created by the factory after a rebalance gets a dead pool with no workers.

Unbounded queues give no backpressure; docstring claims otherwise

The queues are unbounded and `submit` never blocks or raises `MessageRejected`. The consumer will keep polling Kafka while a slow worker backs up, so memory grows without limit. The class docstring's claim of 'natural backpressure' is false.

get_committable_offsets scans a Python range over offsets

The loop iterates `range(start, max_offset+1)` under a lock every second. If offsets have large gaps (compacted or filtered topics), this becomes a very long loop. A gap also stops commits permanently, since a missing offset is never in all_offsets. For example, a skipped or non-contiguous offset blocks all further commits for that partition.
